messages.subject: Re: Model fit
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris (and list),

There is plenty of discussion and examples showing how to choose detection
function models in the Distance Sampling book, which is available for free
online (http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distancebook/ see, for example, section
3.5 "Choice of model", sections 4.1-4.6, 5.1-5.6, 8.2, 8.3, etc).  If this
still doesn't make sense you may want to think about coming on a workshop (next
ones will be August 2001 in St Andrews http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/icods/).

I'm not sure what you meant about not being able to generate graphs of model
fits for your data in Distance.  I assume you mean Distance 3.5.  Running
analyses in Distance 3.5 is explained in the online manual, under Analyses in
Distance and subsequent pages.

Hope this helps.  If you have specific questions, send them to me rather than
the list and I will respond privately.

 - Len Thomas
   Distance project coordinator

--
Len Thomas (l...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk)
Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Mathematical Institute, University of St Andrews
Scotland

messages.subject: Variance of n
messages.body_plain:
I've been trying for 2 days now to finalize an abundance estimate for
whales. The final estimator is much like that in the example given in 8.5
of the textbook. There is stratification over blocks and two categories of
Beaufort sea state. Hence the final estimates of abundance and variance
must be worked out outside of the Distance program, as it cannot handle two
levels of stratification.

My problem has been the calculation of the variance of the total population
estimate, N. I have followed closely the example given on p. 388-390 of the
text, but have not been able to derive an answer that seems reasonable. I
suspect I am doing something very basically wrong, and my prime suspect is
my calculation of var(n), where n is the number of sightings. This is
required for the calculation.

On a basic level, I do not actually understand how n can have a variance,
since it is not estimated. However n/L (encounter rate) does certainly have
a variance. My assumption has been that var(n) can be calculated by scaling
the SE of n/L by L, then squaring. But perhaps I am wrong about this?

I am sorry if this seems a trivial question.

Best regards,

Daniel Pike

messages.subject: Re: Variance of n
messages.body_plain:
> > On a basic level, I do not actually understand how n can have a variance,
> > since it is not estimated. However n/L (encounter rate) does certainly have
> > a variance. My assumption has been that var(n) can be calculated by scaling
> > the SE of n/L by L, then squaring. But perhaps I am wrong about this?

Daniel, the material you need is on p90 of the book.  Note that you need a
weighted sample variance of encounter rate, weighted by line length.  As n
is just a constant (L) times the encounter rate, clearly it can have a
variance.  It is an estimator of the expected sample size, E(n) (see for
example p87, 105, 116.

With best wishes,

Steve

messages.subject: Badgers
messages.body_plain:
Dear Distance users,

I am working on a project that needs to estimate the density of European
Badgers (Meles meles). There are two questions that have arisen from
this.

1. In our study area the badgerÕs setts are invariably in woodland, but
the majority of their foraging is done on surrounding fields. Using
spotlights on open land is very effective so there is no problem there.
The woodland, however does pose significant problems. Observing badgers
in woodland is extremely rare and a spotlight is almost a hindrance due
to the shadows it throws.

The question is: Can we estimate the population for the whole area by
just sampling the open land? We have an idea but I thought it would be
prudent to check with the experts first.

What we do know: a) the total area of the site, b) the area of the
woodland, and c) the area of open land. We can also assume that the each
individual will forage on the open land most nights. Is it right assume
that the population estimate derived from just sampling the open land,
will be an accurate estimate of the population for the total area? i.e.
a higher density estimate but less area (just open land) as opposed to a
lower density and a bigger area(open land plus woodland). What would the
limitations of this approach be?

2. Badgers live in extended family groups and maintain fairly strict
territories. Obviously when they first emerge from the sett in the
evening they are concentrated in a small area. How should the sampling
account for this. Our approach is to wait until two hours or so after
the emergence to allow them to spread as homogeneously as possible. Is
there any other considerations to be aware of? Is there any problems
with the territorial nature of these animals?

I hope this mail is clear, and IÕll look forward to any suggestions.

Regards,

Tim Hounsome.

--

messages.subject: Re: Badgers
messages.body_plain:
> > 1. In our study area the badgerÕs setts are invariably in woodland, but
> > the majority of their foraging is done on surrounding fields. Using
> > spotlights on open land is very effective so there is no problem there.
> > The woodland, however does pose significant problems. Observing badgers
> > in woodland is extremely rare and a spotlight is almost a hindrance due
> > to the shadows it throws.
> >
> > The question is: Can we estimate the population for the whole area by
> > just sampling the open land? We have an idea but I thought it would be
> > prudent to check with the experts first.
> >
> > What we do know: a) the total area of the site, b) the area of the
> > woodland, and c) the area of open land. We can also assume that the each
> > individual will forage on the open land most nights. Is it right assume
> > that the population estimate derived from just sampling the open land,
> > will be an accurate estimate of the population for the total area? i.e.
> > a higher density estimate but less area (just open land) as opposed to a
> > lower density and a bigger area(open land plus woodland). What would the
> > limitations of this approach be?

This approach works provided all badgers are in open country at the time
you survey.  If not, then you estimate only that part of the population
that is in the open area.  It doesn't matter if you include or exclude the
woodland area in your calculation.  If you include it, you get an average
density across woodland and open land; as the woodland density is assumed
to be zero (no badgers seen there), that will give you a lower density
than if you exclude it - but then you multiply by a larger overall area,
which compensates.  If, as seems more realistic, some badgers occur in
woodland, you ideally need supplementary studies to estimate the
proportion in woodland at the time of the surveys -
e.g. radio-tagging.  Failing that, you can adjust the area surveyed around
points to take account of areas that are not visible, but you then have to
assume that density in woodland is the same as elsewhere, so that approach
isn't worth pursuing.

> > 2. Badgers live in extended family groups and maintain fairly strict
> > territories. Obviously when they first emerge from the sett in the
> > evening they are concentrated in a small area. How should the sampling
> > account for this. Our approach is to wait until two hours or so after
> > the emergence to allow them to spread as homogeneously as possible. Is
> > there any other considerations to be aware of? Is there any problems
> > with the territorial nature of these animals?

That seems a good strategy.  Clustering doesn't matter, except it reduces
precision a little, so giving them time to disperse will improve precision
... and possibly reduce the numbers that remain in woodland.

Steve

> > What we do know: a) the total area of the site, b) the area of the
> > woodland, and c) the area of open land. We can also assume that the each
> > individual will forage on the open land most nights. Is it right assume
> > that the population estimate derived from just sampling the open land,
> > will be an accurate estimate of the population for the total area? i.e.
> > a higher density estimate but less area (just open land) as opposed to a
> > lower density and a bigger area(open land plus woodland). What would the
> > limitations of this approach be?

This approach works provided all badgers are in open country at the time
you survey.  If not, then you estimate only that part of the population
that is in the open area.  It doesn't matter if you include or exclude the
woodland area in your calculation.  If you include it, you get an average
density across woodland and open land; as the woodland density is assumed
to be zero (no badgers seen there), that will give you a lower density
than if you exclude it - but then you multiply by a larger overall area,
which compensates.  If, as seems more realistic, some badgers occur in
woodland, you ideally need supplementary studies to estimate the
proportion in woodland at the time of the surveys -
e.g. radio-tagging.  Failing that, you can adjust the area surveyed around
points to take account of areas that are not visible, but you then have to
assume that density in woodland is the same as elsewhere, so that approach
isn't worth pursuing.

> > 2. Badgers live in extended family groups and maintain fairly strict
> > territories. Obviously when they first emerge from the sett in the
> > evening they are concentrated in a small area. How should the sampling
> > account for this. Our approach is to wait until two hours or so after
> > the emergence to allow them to spread as homogeneously as possible. Is
> > there any other considerations to be aware of? Is there any problems
> > with the territorial nature of these animals?

That seems a good strategy.  Clustering doesn't matter, except it reduces
precision a little, so giving them time to disperse will improve precision
... and possibly reduce the numbers that remain in woodland.

Steve

messages.subject: Re: Badgers
messages.body_plain:
Tim,

I would suggest that it would be much simpler to use some sort of cue
counting method using dung pits, latrines and even better - setts themselves
(you could stratify by the number of holes or the size of the mound etc).

Without knowing exactly what you are doing, it is hard to give any more
advice. I would suggest reviewing your aims and establishing whether
Distance is the right method to use. I apologise in advance if this is
telling you what you already know and there are good reasons why you would
not want to use these methods (not knowing more about the aims of the
project), but.....

Probably better to identify all known setts and feeding tracks etc (there
are standard methods for doing this and it is possible to identify different
clans by bait marking etc - quite intensive study but much simpler to get an
overview). I would then suggest that you concentrate on each main sett /
annex, identifying if they are active or not and then perhaps counting
individuals as they emerge - again assuming that you are trying to get as
close to an exact population as possible and you are doing a study over a
relatively small area (I know a project that has done this over about 6
square kilometres). If it is part of large scale monitoring, perhaps you
could consider sampling.

It's just a hunch, but I reckon that Distance is not really practical for
this project. Even with a lot of effort, I would doubt that your confidence
limits would be nearly good enough to be of practical use. So much is known
about the life history and behaviour of Badgers that you can design a much
better and more accurate short-term study using other published methods.

Having said that, I would be very interested to know if Distance data on
dung pits and latrines can be correlated with Badger populations / number of
clans. Has anyone done this sort of experiment?

I don't know if this will help, but here are some references:

Cresswell, P., Harris, S. & Jefferies, D. J. (1990) The history,
distribution, status and habitat requirements of the badger in Britain.
JNCC, Peterborough.
Harris, S., Jefferies, D., Cheeseman, C. & Booty, C. (1994) Problems with
Badgers? RSPCA, Horsham.

Regards,

Simon Mustoe.

-----Original Message-----
From: Tim Hounsome <t.hou...@csl.gov.uk>
To: distance...@mailbase.ac.uk <distance...@mailbase.ac.uk>
Date: 26 October 2000 11:59
Subject: Badgers

Dear Distance users,

I am working on a project that needs to estimate the density of European
Badgers (Meles meles). There are two questions that have arisen from
this.

1. In our study area the badgerÕs setts are invariably in woodland, but
the majority of their foraging is done on surrounding fields. Using
spotlights on open land is very effective so there is no problem there.
The woodland, however does pose significant problems. Observing badgers
in woodland is extremely rare and a spotlight is almost a hindrance due
to the shadows it throws.

The question is: Can we estimate the population for the whole area by
just sampling the open land? We have an idea but I thought it would be
prudent to check with the experts first.

What we do know: a) the total area of the site, b) the area of the
woodland, and c) the area of open land. We can also assume that the each
individual will forage on the open land most nights. Is it right assume
that the population estimate derived from just sampling the open land,
will be an accurate estimate of the population for the total area? i.e.
a higher density estimate but less area (just open land) as opposed to a
lower density and a bigger area(open land plus woodland). What would the
limitations of this approach be?

2. Badgers live in extended family groups and maintain fairly strict
territories. Obviously when they first emerge from the sett in the
evening they are concentrated in a small area. How should the sampling
account for this. Our approach is to wait until two hours or so after
the emergence to allow them to spread as homogeneously as possible. Is
there any other considerations to be aware of? Is there any problems
with the territorial nature of these animals?

I hope this mail is clear, and IÕll look forward to any suggestions.

Regards,

Tim Hounsome.

messages.subject: Bird Density vs Relative Abundance comparisons
messages.subject_clean: Bird Density vs Relative Abundance comparisons
messages.body_plain:
Greetings-

We've analyzed bird data for a large scale (with inference to the State of Utah, USA, ~22,000,000 ha), long-term (9 years to date) population monitoring program, and we are in the process of writing a short methodological comparison paper, examining the different conclusions of the two analysis methods ('traditional' relative abundance vs density using DISTANCE).

I'd like to poll DISTANCE users as to: what sorts of comparisons are likely to be meaningful, given that a) we've no standard of 'truth' with which to make reference, and b) it seems to me that the very scale of the relative abundance information is suspect (i.e., it is not rooted to a known area, unless one assumes perfect detectability out to the plot radius which is obviously incorrect).  Your opinions, epistles, or monographs are welcomed.

-Russ

messages.subject: Distribution issue
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I am trying to implement DISTANCE overhere, and I constantly get asked about
the
underlying distribution assumption (uniform, random) for counted animals and
for transects to make DISTANCE work and get reliable results.

Apparently, the distribution of objects is not very relevant, as long as the
transect line
is placed randomly (does the argument also work vice versa ?).

In lots of studies, e.g. at-sea counts from a ferry, repeated transects or
narrow fjords, one has no real impact on the transect location.

So my question then is, how much does the above really matter, and how can
one argue and/or correct, if necessary ?

 Thanks and best reagrds

messages.subject: Re: zero values analyzed as 4th species
messages.body_plain:
Hi Genisis,

> >1.) In my observation layer, I am post stratifying by species. I am
> >including line transect censuses that did not have any sightings.
> >Distance is treating these no sightings (no matter if they are entered
> >as "0" or "default") as a fourth species, and I am afraid this is
> >biasing my results. How can I tell Distance not to analyze zero values
> >as a forth species?

Line transects that did not have any sightings should not have any records in
the Observation layer.  They should not be "0" or "default".  For an example,
see the online help, Users Guide page "Data in Distance - Data Structure".
There is a picture there of a data sheet (3rd picture down), in which there
are no observations for line transect numbers 9, 10, 11, 12.

If this still doesn't make sense to you, and you have read the Users Guide
carefully from cover to cover, then please send me a copy of your distance
project file, zipped up and I will edit it to show you what I mean.  (please
send to me privately: dist...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk , not to the list.)

> >2.) Results are showing that my f(0), p, and ESW is exactly the same for
> >all three species, including my zero values (the imaginary fourth
> >species).  Why is this happening, and how can I fix it?

You need to estimate the detection function by stratum.  You do this in the
Model Definition, Estimate tab - there is a box half way down where you can
check the "Detection Function" line, "Stratum" column.  See online help page
"Model Definition Properties - Estiamte"

> >3.) Also, although this question may arise more from my ignorance than
> >anything else, how can I have a detection probability greater than 1, or
> >100%? The first histogram bar on Plot three rises to a detection
> >probability of 1.54. Do I ignore that and just look at my red function
> >line (which does rise to exactly 1)?

Yes, the labelling on this graph is a bit confusing.  The line shows the
estimated detection probability (which is 1 at disance = 0), while the
histograms are the frequency that objects are observed in each band, scaled
so that the observed number is equal to the estimated number over all the
bands.  If you look at the next page of output (the goodness-of-fit tests)
you can see the actual numbers observed and expected in each of the bands.

There is a little bit about the outputs in the online manual under "Brief
Analysis Guidelines", but I should probably put more explanations about the
plots in there in the next version.

Hope this helps,

 - Len Thomas

--

Scotland

messages.body_plain:
Hello Steve Buckland and Distance users,

I am working on finding the density, detection function, and effective
strip width of three species of primates in La Selva National Park,
Costa Rica. It's taken a while to learn the program, but I think I've
gotten as far as I can, so I am writing now in the hopes that any of you
might know the answers to the following questions:

1.) In my observation layer, I am post stratifying by species. I am
including line transect censuses that did not have any sightings.
Distance is treating these no sightings (no matter if they are entered
as "0" or "default") as a fourth species, and I am afraid this is
biasing my results. How can I tell Distance not to analyze zero values
as a forth species?

2.) Results are showing that my f(0), p, and ESW is exactly the same for
all three species, including my zero values (the imaginary fourth
species).  Why is this happening, and how can I fix it?

3.) Also, although this question may arise more from my ignorance than
anything else, how can I have a detection probability greater than 1, or
100%? The first histogram bar on Plot three rises to a detection
probability of 1.54. Do I ignore that and just look at my red function
line (which does rise to exactly 1)?

Any help you can offer would be greatly appreciated.

Sincerely,
Genesis Humphrey

messages.subject: Re: Distribution issue
messages.body_plain:
Hi Falk,

You're right - it is not important that the objects be randomly (ie Poisson)
distributed (Distance Sampling book, page 18).  Rather the transect lines or
points need to be placed randomly with respect to the distribution of
objects.  A simple random survey design achieves this, but in practice we
often use a systematic design with random start point.

There are many cases of studies where the count locations are not placed
according to such a design, as you mentioned.  In these cases it is no
problem to estimate the density or abundance of objects in the surveyed area
(ie the area where the transects were).  The problem comes when you try to
extrapolate this abundance to the whole study area.  For example, if you have
at-sea counts of cetaceans from a ferry, you could hope to reliably estimate
the density of cetaceans on the ferry route.  What this tells you about the
cetacean population in the sea that the ferry crosses is another matter.

In these circumstances you have two choices: (1) assume that the transects
are representative of the whole area and use the normal design-based estimate
(ie the same estimate that we use when transects are placed at random); or
(2) use spatial modelling to provide a model-based estimate of the abundance,
using relevant covariables such as (in the ferry example) sea bottom depth,
current speed, latitude, longitude, etc.  Neither is guarenteed to be
reliable however.

messages.subject: Re: Distribution issue
messages.body_plain:
Hi Falk,

You're right - it is not important that the objects be randomly (ie Poisson)
distributed (Distance Sampling book, page 18).  Rather the transect lines or
points need to be placed randomly with respect to the distribution of
objects.  A simple random survey design achieves this, but in practice we
often use a systematic design with random start point.

There are many cases of studies where the count locations are not placed
according to such a design, as you mentioned.  In these cases it is no
problem to estimate the density or abundance of objects in the surveyed area
(ie the area where the transects were).  The problem comes when you try to
extrapolate this abundance to the whole study area.  For example, if you have
at-sea counts of cetaceans from a ferry, you could hope to reliably estimate
the density of cetaceans on the ferry route.  What this tells you about the
cetacean population in the sea that the ferry crosses is another matter.

In these circumstances you have two choices: (1) assume that the transects
are representative of the whole area and use the normal design-based estimate
(ie the same estimate that we use when transects are placed at random); or
(2) use spatial modelling to provide a model-based estimate of the abundance,
using relevant covariables such as (in the ferry example) sea bottom depth,
current speed, latitude, longitude, etc.  Neither is guarenteed to be
reliable however.

Perhaps someone on the list could suggest suitable references to papers that
compare design and model based estimation?  I can recommend the following:

Buckland, Goudie and Borchers.  2000. Wildlife population assessment: past
developments and future directions.  Biometrics 56: 1-12.  [There is a short
section in here comparing design and model based inference and providing
references.]

the topic.]
